histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What is the routine fixative used for histology, and what does it do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: 10% neutral-buffered formalin — it cross-links proteins, halts autolysis and bacterial decay, and hardens the tissue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: List the steps of the standard tissue-processing pipeline in order.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Fixation → dehydration (graded alcohols) → clearing (xylene) → embedding (paraffin wax) → microtomy (3–5 µm sections) → rehydrate, stain (usually H&E) and mount under a coverslip.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Why is tissue dehydrated and cleared before embedding?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Graded alcohols remove water; xylene (the clearing agent) then removes the alcohol so molten paraffin wax can infiltrate the tissue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: At what thickness are routine paraffin sections cut?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: 3–5 µm.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What is a frozen section and when is it used?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Tissue is snap-frozen and cut on a cryostat, skipping wax — gives a diagnosis in minutes (e.g. intra-operative margin assessment) and is the main way to preserve lipids and many enzymes, at the cost of poorer morphology.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does haematoxylin stain, and what colour?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: It is a basic dye that binds acidic (basophilic) structures — nuclei/chromatin, RER and ribosomes — staining them blue–purple.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does eosin stain, and what colour?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: It is an acidic dye that binds basic (eosinophilic/acidophilic) structures — cytoplasmic proteins, collagen, muscle, RBCs and keratin — staining them pink.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does 'basophilic' mean on an H&E slide?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Structures that bind the basic dye haematoxylin because they are acidic/negatively charged (nucleic acids) — they appear blue (nuclei, RER, ribosomes).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Why does a plasma cell (or pancreatic acinar cell) have blue cytoplasm?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Its cytoplasm is packed with rough ER/ribosomes (RNA), which is acidic and therefore basophilic — 'blue = nucleic-acid–rich', i.e. a cell busy making protein.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: PAS stain: target and colour?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Glycogen, basement membranes, mucins and fungi → magenta. Adding diastase removes glycogen; if the magenta disappears it confirms the substance was glycogen (PAS-D).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does Masson's trichrome show?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Collagen stains blue/green and muscle/cytoplasm stains red — used to grade fibrosis (e.g. cirrhosis).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does a reticulin (silver) stain highlight?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Reticular (type III collagen) fibres as a black mesh — shows the architecture of liver, bone marrow and lymph node.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does an elastic stain (Verhoeff/EVG) show?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Elastic fibres, staining them black — useful in elastic arteries and skin; elastic loss is seen in aneurysm.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Perls' Prussian blue stains what?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Ferric iron / haemosiderin — blue. Used in haemochromatosis and to show old haemorrhage.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which stain identifies amyloid, and what is the diagnostic finding?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Congo red — amyloid shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which stain demonstrates acid-fast bacilli, and in what disease?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Ziehl–Neelsen — acid-fast bacilli appear as red rods on a blue background; classic for TB and other mycobacteria.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which stain is used for blood/marrow films and organisms like H. pylori?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Giemsa (or Wright) stain.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which stains show lipids, and what is the catch?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Oil Red O / Sudan stains lipid red — but they require frozen tissue, because the alcohols/xylene used in processing dissolve fat.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does toluidine blue show and by what phenomenon?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Mast-cell granules — via metachromasia, staining the granules purple rather than blue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Name the three special stains most likely to be tested and their targets.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back:
• Congo red → amyloid (apple-green birefringence)
  • Ziehl–Neelsen → TB (acid-fast bacilli)
  • PAS → fungi and basement membrane

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What is immunohistochemistry (IHC) used for?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: It uses labelled antibodies to detect specific antigens, answering 'what kind of cell is this?' — especially to classify a tumour of uncertain origin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which IHC marker indicates an epithelial tumour (carcinoma)?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Cytokeratins (CK).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What do CD45 (LCA) and S100 mark on IHC?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: CD45 → leucocytes (lymphoma); S100 → melanoma, nerve and cartilage.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does Ki-67 indicate, and why do ER/PR/HER2 matter?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Ki-67 = proliferation index (tumour grade). ER/PR/HER2 classify breast cancer and guide therapy (e.g. HER2-positive → trastuzumab).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What is the correct order for approaching a slide?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Low power first (orientation & architecture) → medium power (functional unit & epithelium) → high power (cell types, nuclei, specialisations). Architecture before cytology.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What do you assess at low power?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Overall architecture — is there a capsule; is the pattern a layered tube, lobules, follicles or tubules — to make a first guess at the organ.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What are the four questions that name most tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back:
• (1) Epithelium or connective tissue?
  • (2) Simple or stratified?
  • (3) Cell shape — squamous, cuboidal or columnar?
  • (4) Surface specialisation — cilia, brush border or keratin?

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: How is total magnification calculated on a light microscope, and what is its resolution limit?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Total magnification = objective × eyepiece (e.g. 40× × 10× = 400×); useful up to ~1000× with a resolution limit of ~0.2 µm, set by the wavelength of light.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does TEM show that light microscopy cannot?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Ultrastructure — organelles, basement membrane, cell junctions and the cilia axoneme (9+2), with resolution down to ~0.2 nm.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Give two situations where electron microscopy is needed for diagnosis.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: A renal filtration-barrier lesion (podocyte foot processes, GBM) and primary ciliary dyskinesia (absent axonemal dynein arms).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Name three common histological artefacts.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back:
• Folds/tears
  • knife (chatter) marks
  • shrinkage clefts
  • air bubbles
  • formalin pigment
  • or freezing artefact
— any three.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does a routine biopsy report on an H&E slide?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back:
• Cell type
  • grade
  • resection margins
  • and presence of invasion.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Why are graded (increasing-strength) alcohols used for dehydration rather than straight absolute alcohol?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: To dehydrate gradually and avoid the tissue distortion/shrinkage that abrupt full-strength alcohol would cause.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What is metachromasia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: When a dye stains a tissue component a different colour from the dye itself — e.g. toluidine blue stains mast-cell granules and cartilage GAGs purple.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which silver stain is used for fungi as an alternative to PAS?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS), which stains fungal walls black.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What is the difference between immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Both use antibodies against specific antigens; IHC uses an enzyme/chromogen visible by light microscopy, immunofluorescence uses a fluorescent label viewed under a fluorescence microscope (e.g. renal/skin biopsies).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What embedding medium is used for frozen sections, and why are they fast?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Tissue is embedded in OCT compound and frozen, then cut on a cryostat — no lengthy fixation/wax processing, so a result is available in minutes.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does 'acidophilic' mean regarding dye charge?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: An acidophilic (eosinophilic) structure is basic/positively charged and binds the acidic dye eosin, staining pink.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Why does a tissue's calcium content prevent routine sectioning, and what is done?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Calcified matrix is too hard for the microtome, so calcified tissue (e.g. bone) must be decalcified with acid or EDTA first.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What is the auramine–rhodamine stain used for?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: A fluorescent stain for acid-fast bacilli (an alternative to Ziehl–Neelsen for detecting mycobacteria such as TB).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does a tissue Gram (Brown–Brenn) stain demonstrate?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Bacteria within tissue — Gram-positive organisms stain violet, Gram-negative organisms stain pink/red.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does Alcian blue stain, and what is the Alcian blue–PAS (AB–PAS) combination used for?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Alcian blue stains acidic mucins/glycosaminoglycans blue. AB–PAS separates acidic (blue) from neutral (magenta) mucins — e.g. demonstrating goblet cells/intestinal metaplasia in Barrett's oesophagus.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What does mucicarmine stain?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Epithelial mucin rose-red — helps identify adenocarcinoma, and classically stains the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which stains demonstrate calcium deposits in tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Von Kossa (calcium salts black) and Alizarin red S (calcium orange-red).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What organisms does a Warthin–Starry (silver) stain show?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Spirochaetes (e.g. Treponema pallidum in syphilis); it also demonstrates Bartonella and Helicobacter pylori.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: Which organism is classically shown by Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) in an immunocompromised patient?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Pneumocystis jirovecii — black, cup/helmet-shaped cysts (Pneumocystis pneumonia, PCP); GMS also stains fungi generally.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.front: What fixation and processing does electron microscopy require?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.back: Glutaraldehyde (with osmium tetroxide as a secondary fixative/lipid stain), resin embedding and ultrathin (~60–90 nm) sections — not routine formalin and paraffin wax.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What type of tissue is bone, and what is its defining feature?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: A specialised connective tissue whose defining feature is a calcified (mineralised) extracellular matrix — this makes it rigid, unlike any other connective tissue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What are the two components of bone matrix and roughly what proportion is each?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Organic osteoid (~35%) and inorganic mineral (~65%).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the organic matrix (osteoid) made of, and what does it provide?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Mainly type I collagen (~90%) plus non-collagen proteins — osteocalcin (a vitamin-K-dependent Gla protein), osteonectin and osteopontin; it provides tensile strength and flexibility.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the inorganic component of bone, its formula, and its role?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2 — provides compressive strength and hardness, and acts as the body's mineral store.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: List the main functions of bone.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back:
• Support & protection
  • movement (levers/muscle attachment)
  • mineral reservoir (~99% of body calcium and ~85% of phosphate → Ca2+ homeostasis)
  • haematopoiesis (houses marrow)
  • and endocrine roles (osteocalcin, FGF23).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Using the reinforced-concrete analogy, what do collagen and hydroxyapatite each represent?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Collagen = the steel rods (resist tension/stretching); hydroxyapatite = the concrete (resists compression). Lose mineral → rubbery bone (osteomalacia); weaken collagen → brittle bone (osteogenesis imperfecta).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the structural (functional) unit of compact bone?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: The osteon (Haversian system) — concentric lamellae around a central Haversian canal.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What do the Haversian and Volkmann's canals contain and how are they oriented?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Both carry neurovascular bundles: Haversian canals run longitudinally at the centre of osteons; Volkmann's (perforating) canals run transversely, connecting Haversian canals to each other and to the periosteum.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What are interstitial and circumferential lamellae?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Interstitial lamellae are remnants of old, partially resorbed osteons filling the gaps between osteons; circumferential lamellae line the outer and inner bone surfaces.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: How does cancellous (spongy) bone differ structurally from compact bone?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Cancellous bone is a network of thin trabeculae with marrow-filled spaces and NO osteons (trabeculae are nourished by diffusion from marrow); trabeculae align along lines of stress (Wolff's law).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Why is cancellous bone affected first in osteoporosis?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: It has ~20% of skeletal mass but ~90% of the surface area, so it is metabolically active with high turnover — making it the first to be lost.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is Wolff's law?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Bone (especially trabeculae) remodels and aligns itself along the lines of mechanical stress it experiences.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Name the four bone cell types.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back:
• Osteoprogenitor
  • osteoblast
  • osteocyte
  • and osteoclast.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Describe the osteoblast: origin, appearance and function.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Derived from mesenchymal osteoprogenitors; cuboidal with basophilic cytoplasm (abundant RER); secretes osteoid and initiates mineralisation, lining bone surfaces.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is an osteocyte and what is its key role?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: A mature osteoblast trapped in a lacuna, with processes running through canaliculi; it maintains the matrix and acts as a mechanosensor directing remodelling.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Describe the osteoclast: lineage, appearance and how it resorbs bone.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: A large multinucleated cell of monocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineage; sits in Howship's lacunae; its ruffled border secretes H+ (dissolves mineral) and cathepsin K (digests collagen).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Which bone cell is of haematopoietic origin, and which are mesenchymal?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Only the osteoclast is haematopoietic (monocyte/macrophage line); osteoprogenitor, osteoblast and osteocyte are mesenchymal.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Explain the RANK–RANKL–OPG axis.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Osteoblasts and osteocytes (the principal adult source) express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive osteoclast formation/activation; OPG is a decoy receptor that blocks this. PTH and vitamin D raise RANKL → more resorption. Denosumab is an anti-RANKL drug.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Compare periosteum and endosteum.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Periosteum covers the external surface (outer fibrous + inner osteogenic layer, anchored by Sharpey's fibres, vascular and sensory); endosteum is a thin lining of internal surfaces — medullary cavity, Haversian canals and trabeculae.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What are Sharpey's fibres?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Collagen fibres that anchor the periosteum (and tendons/ligaments) to the underlying bone.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Contrast woven and lamellar bone.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Woven bone is immature — laid down rapidly with random collagen, more cells and weaker (fetal skeleton, fracture callus, Paget's). Lamellar bone is mature — organised parallel/concentric collagen and stronger, and progressively replaces woven bone.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is intramembranous ossification and which bones form this way?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Bone forms directly from mesenchyme (osteoblasts) with no cartilage model — the flat bones: skull vault, most facial bones, clavicle and mandible.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is endochondral ossification and which bones form this way?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: A hyaline cartilage model is replaced by bone — long bones, vertebrae, base of skull and most of the skeleton; via a primary (diaphysis) and secondary (epiphyseal) ossification centres.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Name the five zones of the epiphyseal growth plate in order.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Resting/reserve → Proliferation → Hypertrophy → Calcification → Ossification.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Distinguish longitudinal from appositional bone growth.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Longitudinal (length) growth occurs at the epiphyseal growth plate and stops when it fuses after puberty; appositional (width) growth is added by osteoblasts from the periosteum.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the Basic Multicellular Unit (BMU) and roughly how much bone is remodelled yearly?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: The coupled team of osteoclasts (resorb) then osteoblasts (form) that renews bone; about 10% of the skeleton is replaced per year.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What are the purposes of bone remodelling?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back:
• Repair of microdamage
  • adaptation to mechanical load (Wolff's law)
  • and calcium homeostasis.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the net effect of PTH on bone and serum calcium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: PTH increases resorption indirectly (via osteoblast RANKL) → raises serum Ca2+. Intermittent low-dose PTH is paradoxically anabolic (teriparatide).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the role of calcitriol (vitamin D) in bone, and what happens in deficiency?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: It increases gut absorption of calcium and phosphate, enabling matrix mineralisation; deficiency causes osteomalacia (adults) or rickets (children).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Why does menopause cause bone loss?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Oestrogen normally restrains osteoclastic resorption; its loss at menopause accelerates resorption → post-menopausal osteoporosis.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Which stains distinguish mineralised bone from unmineralised osteoid?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: von Kossa (mineral black) and Goldner's trichrome (mineralised bone green, osteoid red) — the latter is used to diagnose osteomalacia by its wide red osteoid seams.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is tetracycline labelling used for?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: It binds the mineralisation front and fluoresces; a double label lets you measure the bone-formation rate (dynamic histomorphometry).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: How does osteoporosis differ from osteomalacia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Osteoporosis = reduced bone MASS with normal mineralisation (resorption > formation). Osteomalacia = defective MINERALISATION with excess unmineralised osteoid (usually vitamin D deficiency).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the histological hallmark of Paget's disease of bone?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: A mosaic pattern of cement lines from disordered, excessive remodelling, producing enlarged but structurally weak bone.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Outline the stages of fracture healing.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Haematoma → soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus → hard (woven-bone) callus → remodelling to mature lamellar bone.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What are canaliculi and what is their function?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Tiny channels radiating from lacunae that house osteocyte processes, allowing osteocytes to communicate and receive nutrients by diffusion from the central canal.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is osteoid?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: The unmineralised organic matrix (mainly type I collagen + ground substance) secreted by osteoblasts, before hydroxyapatite is deposited.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the role of alkaline phosphatase in bone?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Secreted by osteoblasts, it is a marker of active bone formation and helps initiate matrix mineralisation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the difference between the epiphysis, metaphysis and diaphysis of a long bone?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back:
• Epiphysis = the end (secondary ossification centre)
  • metaphysis = the region adjacent to the growth plate
  • diaphysis = the shaft (primary ossification centre).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is osteitis fibrosa cystica and its cause?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Bone resorption with fibrous replacement and 'brown tumours', caused by hyperparathyroidism (excess PTH-driven osteoclast activity).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is sclerostin, which cell makes it, and its therapeutic relevance?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Sclerostin (SOST gene) is secreted by osteocytes and inhibits Wnt signalling in osteoblasts → less bone formation; mechanical loading lowers sclerostin (a molecular basis for Wolff's law). Romosozumab is an anti-sclerostin anabolic drug.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: How do bisphosphonates work, and how does this differ from denosumab?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: Bisphosphonates (e.g. alendronate) bind hydroxyapatite and are taken up by osteoclasts, inhibiting farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase → osteoclast apoptosis → reduced resorption; denosumab is an anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody. Anabolic alternatives are teriparatide (intermittent PTH) and romosozumab (anti-sclerostin).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Give the serum Ca/PO4/ALP/PTH pattern for osteoporosis, osteomalacia, Paget's and primary hyperparathyroidism.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back:
• Osteoporosis — all normal
  • Osteomalacia/rickets — low/normal Ca, low PO4, high ALP, high PTH (secondary)
  • Paget's — normal Ca and PO4 with a very high (isolated) ALP
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism — high Ca, low PO4, high ALP, high PTH.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: Describe osteosarcoma, the commonest primary bone malignancy.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: A malignant bone-forming tumour with a bimodal age distribution: adolescents (metaphysis of distal femur/proximal tibia) and elderly patients with pre-existing Paget's; X-ray shows a Codman triangle (periosteal elevation) and sunburst spiculation; associated with hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1) and Li-Fraumeni (p53).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is renal osteodystrophy and its mechanism?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: The bone disease of chronic kidney disease: reduced calcitriol synthesis and phosphate retention → hypocalcaemia → secondary (then autonomous tertiary) hyperparathyroidism and high-turnover bone disease; biochemistry shows low Ca, high PO4, high ALP and high PTH.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: How does a secondary osteon form, and what is a cement (reversal) line?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: By a cutting cone — osteoclasts tunnel through old bone and trailing osteoblasts lay down concentric lamellae inward around the new Haversian canal. The cement (reversal) line is a collagen-poor, basophilic boundary marking where resorption stopped; it outlines each osteon, and chaotic cement lines give Paget's its mosaic pattern.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.front: What is the role of carbonic anhydrase II in the osteoclast?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.back: It generates H+ (from CO₂ + water) that the osteoclast's proton pump secretes across the ruffled border to acidify Howship's lacuna and dissolve hydroxyapatite; deficiency causes osteopetrosis (with renal tubular acidosis).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What type of tissue is blood, and what is unusual about its matrix?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: A specialised connective tissue — but uniquely its matrix is a fluid (plasma) rather than solid or gel.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is the difference between plasma and serum?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood (water + proteins including clotting factors); serum is plasma after clotting, i.e. plasma minus fibrinogen and other clotting factors.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Name the three formed elements of blood and their approximate share of blood volume.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Red cells (erythrocytes), white cells (leukocytes) and platelets (thrombocytes) — together ~45% of blood volume; plasma makes up ~55%.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: On centrifuged blood, what are the three layers, and what is the buffy coat?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Packed red cells (bottom), a thin buffy coat of white cells + platelets (middle), and plasma (top). The red-cell fraction is the haematocrit.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Which stain is used for a peripheral blood film, and what are its components?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: A Romanowsky stain (Giemsa, Wright or Leishman) — a mix of acidic eosin (stains basic structures pink/red) and basic methylene blue (stains acidic structures blue/purple).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Where on a blood film should you examine the cells, and why?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: At the feathered edge, where cells form a single layer (monolayer) and morphology is clearest.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Describe the appearance of a normal red blood cell.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: A biconcave disc ~7–8 µm across, anucleate and without organelles, eosinophilic (pink) with a central pallor about one-third of its diameter.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Why is the red cell biconcave and anucleate, and what is the trade-off?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: The biconcave shape maximises surface-area:volume for gas exchange and allows deformability through capillaries; being anucleate leaves maximum room for haemoglobin but means it cannot repair itself — hence a ~120-day lifespan.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: How long do red cells live and where are they removed?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: ~120 days; removed by splenic and hepatic macrophages.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is a reticulocyte and how is it recognised?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: A young red cell still containing residual ribosomal RNA — it appears faintly blue (polychromasia) on a routine film, and a supravital stain (new methylene blue) shows its reticular network. A raised count indicates brisk marrow output.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: How are leukocytes classified into two groups?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Granulocytes / polymorphonuclear (neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil) and agranulocytes / mononuclear (lymphocyte, monocyte).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Describe the neutrophil and its main role.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Commonest WBC (40–75%); multilobed nucleus (2–5 lobes) with fine neutral/lilac granules; phagocytoses bacteria — the key cell of acute bacterial infection.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Describe the eosinophil and its role.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Bilobed nucleus with large red-orange (eosinophilic) granules; acts against parasites (helminths) and in allergy — driving the late-phase allergic reaction rather than the immediate mast-cell/basophil response.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Describe the basophil.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: The rarest WBC (<1%); a bilobed nucleus usually hidden by large dark blue/purple granules containing histamine and heparin; involved in allergy and inflammation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Describe the lymphocyte and its role.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Large, round, dense nucleus with only a thin rim of pale-blue cytoplasm; mediates adaptive immunity — B cells (antibodies), T cells (cell-mediated) and NK cells.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Describe the monocyte and what it becomes.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: The largest WBC; kidney/horseshoe-shaped nucleus with abundant grey-blue cytoplasm; in tissue it becomes a macrophage or dendritic cell (phagocytosis + antigen presentation).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Give the WBC frequency order (commonest to rarest) and a mnemonic.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils — 'Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas'.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is a 'left shift', and what do hypersegmented neutrophils suggest?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: A left shift is an increase in immature band neutrophils, seen in acute infection. Hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes) suggest B12 or folate deficiency.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What are platelets, where do they come from, and what do they do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Anucleate cytoplasmic fragments shed from megakaryocytes (~2–4 µm); they mediate haemostasis — adhering, activating and aggregating into a platelet plug and providing a phospholipid surface for coagulation. Lifespan ~7–10 days.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is haemopoiesis, and where does it occur through life?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: The production of blood cells: yolk sac (early embryo) → liver and spleen (fetal) → red bone marrow (postnatal; in adults the axial skeleton, pelvis and proximal femur/humerus).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: From which cell do all blood cells arise, and what are its two lineages?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: The pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) → a myeloid lineage and a lymphoid lineage.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What does the myeloid lineage produce?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back:
• Erythrocytes
  • granulocytes (neutrophil/eosinophil/basophil)
  • monocytes
  • and (via megakaryocytes) platelets.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What does the lymphoid lineage produce?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: B, T and NK lymphocytes.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Outline erythropoiesis and its driver.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic erythroblast → extrudes its nucleus → reticulocyte → mature RBC; driven by erythropoietin (EPO) from the kidney in response to hypoxia.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What drives granulopoiesis and thrombopoiesis?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Granulopoiesis is driven by G-CSF/GM-CSF; thrombopoiesis (megakaryocyte → platelets) by thrombopoietin (TPO).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is the difference between red and yellow marrow?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Red marrow is active/haematopoietic; yellow marrow is fatty and inactive but can reconvert to red marrow when demand rises (e.g. chronic haemolysis).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: How is bone marrow sampled?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: As an aspirate (for cytology) plus a trephine biopsy (for architecture and cellularity).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Classify anaemia by red-cell size, with a cause for each.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back:
By MCV:
  • microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia)
  • macrocytic — megaloblastic (B12/folate deficiency, with hypersegmented neutrophils) or non-megaloblastic (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis)
  • and normocytic (chronic disease, acute blood loss, haemolysis, renal failure).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What does finding blast cells on a peripheral film suggest?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Acute leukaemia — a haematological emergency.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Which growth factors drive red cells, platelets and neutrophils respectively?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back:
• EPO (kidney) → red cells
  • TPO → platelets
  • G-CSF → neutrophils.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is the normal haematocrit range approximately, and what does it represent?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Roughly 40–54% (men) / 36–48% (women) — the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells after centrifugation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is haemoglobin's role and structure in brief?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: An iron-containing tetramer (2 alpha + 2 beta globin chains, each with a haem group) that binds and transports oxygen; it fills the red cell and gives it its eosinophilia.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is a band (stab) cell?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: An immature neutrophil with a non-segmented, horseshoe-shaped nucleus; increased numbers ('left shift') indicate acute infection.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Which cells make up the granulocytes, and why the alternative name 'polymorphonuclear'?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils; 'polymorphonuclear' refers to their lobed nuclei — the neutrophil is multilobed (2–5 lobes) while eosinophils and basophils are typically bilobed.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is the megakaryocyte and where is it found?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: A very large polyploid marrow cell with a multilobed nucleus that sheds cytoplasmic fragments (platelets) into the sinusoids.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Define anisocytosis and poikilocytosis.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Anisocytosis = variation in red-cell size; poikilocytosis = variation in red-cell shape — both seen in many anaemias.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is the buffy coat used for clinically?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: It concentrates white cells and platelets; it can be sampled for circulating tumour/leukaemic cells or blood parasites that lie outside red cells (microfilariae, trypanosomes). Note malaria parasites are intra-erythrocytic and sought on the whole film, not the buffy coat.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Which lymphocytes are responsible for antibody production versus cell-mediated immunity?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back:
• B lymphocytes (→ plasma cells) make antibodies
  • T lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity
  • NK cells provide innate cytotoxicity.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Which full blood count index separates microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic anaemia, and what is its normal range?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: The MCV (mean cell volume), normally ~80–100 fL: <80 microcytic, 80–100 normocytic, >100 macrocytic.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What are Howell–Jolly bodies and what do they indicate?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Small basophilic nuclear remnants inside red cells; normally removed by the spleen, so their presence indicates hyposplenism or a post-splenectomy state.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Schistocytes (red-cell fragments) on a film suggest what?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Mechanical red-cell destruction — microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (DIC, TTP/HUS) or a mechanical heart valve.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: What is rouleaux formation and its classic association?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Red cells stacked like a pile of coins, caused by a high plasma paraprotein/fibrinogen — classically multiple myeloma (and a raised ESR).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Auer rods and smudge cells each point to which leukaemia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic inclusions in blasts) → acute myeloid leukaemia (AML); smudge/smear cells (fragile lymphocytes) → chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: How does the reticulocyte count help classify anaemia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: A high reticulocyte count means the marrow is responding — blood loss or haemolysis; a low/inappropriately normal count means production failure — marrow disease or haematinic (iron/B12/folate) deficiency.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Reed–Sternberg cells and reactive 'atypical' lymphocytes are each seen in what?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Reed–Sternberg cells (binucleate 'owl-eye' cells) → Hodgkin lymphoma; large atypical/reactive lymphocytes → EBV infectious mononucleosis.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.front: Distinguish reactive thrombocytosis from essential thrombocythaemia.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.back: Reactive thrombocytosis is a secondary rise (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, post-splenectomy) with low thrombotic risk; essential thrombocythaemia is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm that causes both thrombosis and bleeding.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What type of tissue is cartilage, and which three features make it unusual?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: A specialised connective tissue that is avascular, aneural and alymphatic (no blood vessels, nerves or lymphatics).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Why does cartilage heal slowly and poorly?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Because it is avascular — chondrocytes are fed only by diffusion through the matrix, so repair is slow and it tends to degenerate.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What collagen types are found in the three cartilages?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Type II in hyaline and elastic cartilage; predominantly type I (with some type II) in fibrocartilage.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What makes up the ground substance of cartilage, and what does it do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Proteoglycans (mainly aggrecan) and GAGs (chondroitin and keratan sulfate); highly hydrated, so the gel resists compression.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Distinguish chondroblast from chondrocyte.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Chondroblasts secrete matrix at the surface; chondrocytes are the mature cells sitting within the matrix in spaces called lacunae.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What are isogenous groups (cell nests)?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Clusters of 2–4 chondrocytes derived from a single dividing cell — evidence of interstitial growth.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What is the perichondrium and what does it do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: A dense connective-tissue sheath (outer fibrous + inner chondrogenic layer) covering most cartilage; it provides nutrition and is the source of appositional (surface) growth.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Which cartilages have NO perichondrium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Fibrocartilage and articular hyaline cartilage.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Contrast interstitial and appositional growth of cartilage.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Interstitial = chondrocytes divide within the matrix (growth from inside, e.g. growth plate); appositional = new cartilage added at the surface from the perichondrium (growth from outside).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Give the key features and main locations of hyaline cartilage.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Type II collagen (masked/glassy); the commonest cartilage; resists compression; found at articular surfaces, costal cartilage, trachea/bronchi, larynx, nose, the epiphyseal growth plate and the fetal skeleton.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Give the key features and locations of elastic cartilage.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Type II collagen plus abundant elastic fibres → flexible with recoil; found in the external ear (pinna), epiglottis and auditory (Eustachian) tube.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Give the key features and locations of fibrocartilage.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Predominantly type I collagen (with some type II) in thick visible bundles with few chondrocytes in rows; no perichondrium; great tensile strength; found in intervertebral discs (annulus fibrosus), pubic symphysis, knee menisci, TMJ and some tendon/ligament insertions.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Which cartilage forms the fetal skeletal model and the epiphyseal growth plate?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Hyaline cartilage.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: How do you recognise cartilage on a slide?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back:
• Chondrocytes in lacunae (often shrunken)
  • isogenous groups
  • a basophilic matrix with darker territorial matrix around lacunae
  • and (usually) a perichondrium at the edge.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Why is the cartilage matrix basophilic on H&E, and why does hyaline look 'glassy'?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: The sulfated GAGs are acidic and bind haematoxylin (basophilia); type II collagen has the same refractive index as the ground substance so it is masked, giving hyaline its glassy homogeneous look.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Which stains highlight cartilage GAGs/proteoglycans?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Toluidine blue / methylene blue (metachromasia — purple), Alcian blue and safranin O (proteoglycans).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: How is elastic cartilage confirmed histologically?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: With an elastic stain (Verhoeff or orcein), which reveals the network of elastic fibres.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What happens in osteoarthritis at the tissue level?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Progressive loss of articular hyaline cartilage with proteoglycan depletion; repair is poor because cartilage is avascular.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: In disc herniation, which cartilage is involved?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: The nucleus pulposus herniates through the fibrocartilaginous annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What is relapsing polychondritis?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: An autoimmune attack on cartilage causing inflamed, floppy ears that spare the fibrofatty ear lobe, a saddle-nose deformity (septal cartilage destruction) and airway collapse.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Which gene and structure are affected in achondroplasia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: An FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation (autosomal dominant, often de novo) that brakes proliferation in the hyaline growth plate, impairing endochondral ossification → short-limb dwarfism with a normal-length trunk.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What is the territorial matrix of cartilage?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: The more basophilic, GAG-rich rim of matrix immediately surrounding each chondrocyte/lacuna (vs the paler interterritorial matrix further away).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Name the four zones of articular cartilage from surface to bone.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Superficial/tangential (flat cells, collagen parallel — resists shear) → middle/transitional → deep/radial (chondrocyte columns, collagen perpendicular) → calcified zone (below the tidemark, anchoring to subchondral bone).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Why does articular cartilage lack a perichondrium, and what is the consequence?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: So its smooth surface can articulate freely; without a perichondrium (and being avascular) it has very limited repair capacity.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: How is aggrecan organised in the cartilage matrix, and what is chondronectin?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Aggrecan (core protein + chondroitin/keratan-sulfate GAG chains) binds along a hyaluronan backbone to form huge hydrated aggregates that resist compression; chondronectin is an adhesion glycoprotein anchoring chondrocytes to type II collagen (the cartilage analogue of fibronectin).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Why is cartilage useful as graft tissue and relatively immune-privileged?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Because it is avascular and its chondrocytes are isolated within a dense matrix, immune cells reach it poorly — so nasal, auricular and costal cartilage grafts are well tolerated (the same avascularity is why cartilage heals poorly).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Which cartilage type contains type I collagen, and how does this change its appearance?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Fibrocartilage — its type I collagen forms thick, visible bundles (unlike the masked type II collagen of glassy hyaline cartilage).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What happens to hyaline cartilage matrix with ageing/degeneration?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: It can calcify and lose proteoglycan, contributing to reduced resilience and osteoarthritis.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: What are the two zones of the perichondrium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: An outer fibrous layer and an inner chondrogenic layer (source of appositional growth).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Contrast endochondral and intramembranous ossification.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model with bone (long bones, base of skull, growth plate) — how most bones form; intramembranous ossification forms bone directly within mesenchyme with no cartilage template (flat skull bones, clavicle).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.front: Outline the benign-to-malignant spectrum of cartilage tumours.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.back: Enchondroma (benign, medulla of hand bones; multiple in Ollier disease / Maffucci syndrome) and osteochondroma (commonest benign bone tumour, cartilage-capped bony spur) are benign; chondrosarcoma is malignant, usually in older adults and the axial skeleton/pelvis, and is radio/chemo-resistant so treated by surgery.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: From what embryonic tissue is connective tissue derived, and what is its universal plan?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: From mesenchyme. Its universal plan is cells + extracellular matrix, where matrix = fibres + ground substance.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is the defining difference between connective tissue and epithelium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Connective tissue has sparse cells in abundant matrix; epithelium has densely packed cells with little matrix.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which is the most common connective tissue cell and what does it do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: The fibroblast (fibrocyte when resting) — a spindle-shaped cell that secretes the fibres and ground substance of the matrix.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Describe the adipocyte's appearance.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: A signet-ring cell — a single large lipid droplet pushes the nucleus to the rim (fat dissolves in processing, so it looks empty).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is the origin and role of the macrophage in connective tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Derived from blood monocytes; performs phagocytosis and antigen presentation (part of the mononuclear phagocyte system).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What does the mast cell contain and cause, and how is it stained?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Granules of histamine and heparin; drives allergy/inflammation (type I hypersensitivity); shows metachromasia with toluidine blue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Describe the plasma cell and its function.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back:
• Derived from a B lymphocyte
  • secretes antibodies
  • has a clock-face/cartwheel nucleus, basophilic cytoplasm and a pale perinuclear hof.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Distinguish resident (fixed) from wandering (transient) connective-tissue cells.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Resident cells live in the CT (fibroblast, adipocyte, macrophage, mast cell, stem cells); wandering cells arrive from blood (plasma cells, leukocytes) mainly during inflammation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Name the three fibre types of connective tissue.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Collagen, reticular and elastic fibres.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What are collagen fibres made of and how do they look on H&E?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Mostly type I collagen — the most abundant protein in the body; strong and tensile; eosinophilic (pink) wavy bundles.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What are reticular fibres, where are they found, and how are they stained?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Type III collagen forming a fine branching mesh — the framework/stroma of liver, lymph node and marrow; invisible on H&E, shown black by silver stains.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What are elastic fibres made of, and how are they demonstrated?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Elastin plus fibrillin; they provide stretch and recoil (large arteries, some ligaments) and require an elastic stain (Verhoeff/orcein) to see.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What makes up the ground substance and what does it do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: GAGs (hyaluronic acid, chondroitin/dermatan/keratan sulfate), proteoglycans and adhesive glycoproteins (fibronectin, laminin) plus tissue fluid; it resists compression and is the medium for diffusion between capillaries and cells.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Describe loose (areolar) connective tissue and where it is found.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Loosely arranged fibres of all types, many cell types and abundant ground substance — the general-purpose 'packing material', e.g. the lamina propria beneath epithelia and around vessels/nerves.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Describe dense regular connective tissue and give examples.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Tightly packed parallel collagen bundles with fibroblasts in rows between — great tensile strength in one direction; tendons, ligaments and aponeuroses.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Describe dense irregular connective tissue and give examples.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Collagen bundles running in random directions to resist tension from all directions; dermis, organ capsules, submucosa and periosteum.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is reticular tissue and where is it found?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: A network of reticular (type III) fibres with reticular cells forming the stroma of lymphoid organs and bone marrow.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Contrast white and brown adipose tissue.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: White fat is unilocular (one droplet, rim nucleus) for energy storage, insulation and endocrine signalling (leptin, adiponectin). Brown fat is multilocular (many droplets, central nucleus, many mitochondria) for thermogenesis via UCP1 — prominent in neonates.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: How do you recognise connective tissue on a slide?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Sparse cells in abundant pink matrix, with spindle-shaped fibroblast nuclei along collagen bundles; loose CT shows loosely woven fibres, dense regular shows parallel wavy bundles, adipose shows signet-ring cells.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which stains highlight collagen, reticular fibres and elastic fibres?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back:
• Masson's trichrome (collagen blue/green)
  • reticulin/silver (reticular fibres black)
  • and Verhoeff/orcein elastic stain (elastic fibres black/brown).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Why do adipocytes appear empty on routine sections, and how can lipid be shown?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Fat is dissolved by the alcohols/xylene of routine processing; lipid can be shown with Oil Red O or Sudan on frozen tissue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which connective-tissue disorders are due to a collagen problem?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back:
• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (defective collagen → hypermobile joints, fragile stretchy skin)
  • scurvy (vitamin C deficiency → impaired proline/lysine hydroxylation → unstable collagen)
  • and osteogenesis imperfecta (type I collagen → brittle bones, blue sclerae).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which connective-tissue disorder is due to a fibrillin/elastic defect?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation → weak elastic tissue → aortic aneurysm/dissection, lens dislocation).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is multiple myeloma in connective-tissue terms?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: A malignancy of plasma cells producing excess monoclonal antibody.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is the difference between a fibroblast and a fibrocyte?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: A fibroblast is the active matrix-secreting cell; a fibrocyte is the same cell in a quiescent, less active resting state.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which cell type stores histamine and heparin and shows metachromasia with toluidine blue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: The mast cell.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is the mononuclear phagocyte system?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: The body-wide network of monocyte-derived macrophages (e.g. Kupffer cells in liver, microglia in CNS, osteoclasts in bone, alveolar macrophages).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which glycoproteins of the ground substance mediate cell adhesion to the matrix?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Fibronectin and laminin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is Wharton's jelly?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: The mucous (gelatinous) connective tissue of the umbilical cord — an embryonic-type CT rich in ground substance.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which fibre type is stained black by silver and forms organ frameworks?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: Reticular fibres (type III collagen).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is the main hormone/secretory role of white adipose tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: It is an endocrine organ secreting leptin (satiety) and adiponectin, among other adipokines.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is granulation tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back: The new connective tissue of healing wounds — proliferating fibroblasts, new capillaries and inflammatory cells; its matrix is initially type III collagen, remodelled to stronger type I during maturation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: Which collagen type predominates in bone/skin/tendon, cartilage, reticular tissue, and basement membrane?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back:
• Type I = bone, skin, tendon, ligament (most abundant)
  • Type II = cartilage (and vitreous/nucleus pulposus)
  • Type III = reticular fibres (organ stroma, granulation tissue)
  • Type IV = basement membrane.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What is osteogenesis imperfecta?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back:
A defect of type I collagen (COL1A1/COL1A2) causing
  • brittle bones with recurrent fractures
  • blue sclerae
  • hearing loss
  • and dentinogenesis imperfecta.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.front: What are the mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g. Hurler, Hunter)?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.back:
Inherited lysosomal enzyme deficiencies causing accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in connective tissue —
  • coarse facies
  • organomegaly
  • skeletal dysostosis
  • and (in some) intellectual disability.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What are the three roles of epithelium and from which germ layers does it arise?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: It covers surfaces, lines cavities/tubes and forms glands; it derives from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: List the defining features of epithelium.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back:
• Cellular (packed cells, little matrix)
  • avascular (diffusion nutrition)
  • rests on a basement membrane
  • polarised (apical/lateral/basal)
  • held by cell junctions
  • high regenerative capacity.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: How is an epithelium named?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: By the number of cell layers (simple/stratified/pseudostratified) combined with the shape of the surface cell (squamous/cuboidal/columnar). For stratified epithelium the surface layer names it.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is pseudostratified epithelium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: A single layer in which all cells touch the basement membrane but their nuclei sit at different heights, so it looks layered — classically the ciliated columnar epithelium of the respiratory tract.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Where is simple squamous epithelium found and what is its function?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back:
Diffusion, filtration and lubrication —
  • endothelium (blood vessels)
  • mesothelium (serous membranes)
  • alveoli
  • Bowman's capsule
  • and the loop of Henle (thin segments).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Where is simple cuboidal epithelium found?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back:
• Kidney tubules
  • thyroid follicles
  • small gland ducts
  • and the ovary surface
— for secretion and absorption.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Where is simple columnar epithelium found?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Lining the gut from stomach to rectum, and the gallbladder; it is ciliated in the uterine tube — for absorption and secretion.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Which epithelium lines the respiratory tract, and what two features does it have?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells — cilia sweep mucus, goblet cells secrete it.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Contrast keratinised and non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Keratinised (epidermis) has a dry, dead keratin surface for protection; non-keratinised (oral cavity, oesophagus, vagina) is moist and lacks the surface keratin layer.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Which epithelium lines the bladder and ureters, and how does it behave?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) — it stretches, with dome-shaped umbrella cells that flatten as the bladder fills, while staying impermeable to urine.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is the role of the tight junction (zonula occludens)?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: It seals adjacent cells to block paracellular leakage and maintain apical–basal polarity; made of claudins/occludins.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is a desmosome made of and what does it do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Cadherins linked to keratin intermediate filaments; it forms strong spot-welds for mechanical strength — abundant in the epidermis.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What does a gap junction do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Provides cell-to-cell communication — connexons form channels allowing ions and small molecules to pass between cells.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is the role of the hemidesmosome?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: It anchors the basal surface of the epithelial cell to the basement membrane, via integrins.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What makes up the apical junctional complex?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Tight junction + adherens junction + desmosome (e.g. between enterocytes).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What are microvilli and what do they do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Actin-cored finger-like apical projections (the brush/striated border) that increase surface area for absorption — gut and kidney PCT.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Describe cilia and their internal structure.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Motile apical projections with a 9+2 microtubule axoneme powered by dynein; they sweep mucus and ova along the respiratory tract and uterine tube.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What are stereocilia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Long, non-motile microvilli — found in the epididymis and on cochlear hair cells.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is the structure of the basement membrane, and what is it made by?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Basal lamina (lamina lucida + lamina densa: type IV collagen + laminin, made by the epithelium) plus a reticular lamina (type III collagen from connective tissue); it is PAS-positive.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Name the functions of the basement membrane.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back:
• Attaches epithelium to connective tissue
  • guides regeneration/repair
  • and acts as a filtration barrier (e.g. in the glomerulus).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Name the three polarity domains of an epithelial cell.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back:
• Apical (faces lumen — microvilli/cilia)
  • lateral (carries junctions)
  • and basal (hemidesmosomes onto the basement membrane).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Distinguish exocrine from endocrine glands, and give an example of a unicellular gland.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Exocrine glands secrete via ducts onto a surface (sweat, pancreas); endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into blood (thyroid, islets). A goblet cell is a unicellular exocrine (mucous) gland.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Define the three modes of exocrine secretion with an example each.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back:
• Merocrine/eccrine — exocytosis, cell stays intact (sweat, pancreas)
  • apocrine — apical cytoplasm pinched off (mammary, some sweat)
  • holocrine — whole cell disintegrates (sebaceous gland).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Contrast serous and mucous glandular secretions.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Serous = watery, protein-rich (pancreas, parotid); mucous = viscous mucin (goblet cells, sublingual gland); many glands are mixed.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Which special stain highlights basement membrane, goblet-cell mucin and the brush border?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) — magenta.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Which immunohistochemical marker identifies epithelial cells and hence a carcinoma?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Cytokeratin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is metaplasia, with an epithelial example?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: A reversible change of one mature epithelium into another — e.g. Barrett's oesophagus (squamous → columnar), or respiratory ciliated → squamous in smokers.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is a carcinoma, and name the main subtypes.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back:
A malignant tumour of epithelium (the commonest cancers):
  • squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
  • adenocarcinoma (glandular)
  • and urothelial/transitional cell carcinoma (bladder).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is the defect and consequences in primary ciliary dyskinesia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Defective ciliary dynein arms → immotile cilia → bronchiectasis, infertility and situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What causes pemphigus vulgaris?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Autoantibodies against desmoglein in desmosomes → loss of keratinocyte adhesion → intra-epidermal blisters.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is the difference between endothelium and mesothelium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Both are simple squamous epithelia: endothelium lines blood/lymphatic vessels and the heart; mesothelium lines the serous cavities (pleura, peritoneum, pericardium).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Which epithelium lines the oesophagus, and what protects it?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium — many cell layers protect against abrasion from food.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What are the two components of a compound tubuloacinar gland's architecture?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: A branched duct system and secretory units that are both tubular and acinar (e.g. the pancreas, salivary glands).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Contrast pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Pemphigus vulgaris = anti-desmoglein (desmosome) → flaccid INTRA-epidermal blisters; bullous pemphigoid = anti-hemidesmosome (BP180/BP230) → tense SUB-epidermal blisters (elderly).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Which epithelium lines the uterine (fallopian) tube and why is it ciliated?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Simple columnar epithelium with cilia — the cilia sweep the ovum toward the uterus.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is the clinical importance of epithelial regenerative capacity?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Epithelia turn over rapidly (e.g. gut lining, skin), enabling wound healing but also making them vulnerable to malignant transformation (carcinoma) with repeated injury.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is cystic fibrosis at the epithelial level?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: A mutation in CFTR (the apical epithelial chloride channel) → thick, viscid secretions that obstruct exocrine ducts — recurrent chest infection/bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency; diagnostic raised sweat chloride.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: Which basement-membrane diseases involve type IV collagen?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Alport syndrome (mutant type IV collagen → GBM splitting, haematuria, sensorineural deafness) and Goodpasture disease (anti–type IV collagen antibodies → glomerulonephritis + pulmonary haemorrhage).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What is the 'terminal bar' seen on light microscopy?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: The apical junctional complex (tight + adherens + desmosome) seen as an apicolateral dot between epithelial cells, e.g. enterocytes.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.front: What are basolateral infoldings and where are they prominent?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.back: Deep folds of the basal cell membrane packed with mitochondria that power active ion/water transport; they produce the 'striations' of kidney tubule cells and salivary striated ducts.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What are the three types of muscle, and which is voluntary?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Skeletal, cardiac and smooth. Only skeletal muscle is under voluntary (somatic) control; cardiac and smooth are involuntary.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What is the universal contractile machinery shared by all muscle types?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: ATP-powered sliding of actin (thin) and myosin (thick) filaments, triggered by a rise in cytosolic Ca2+.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Define sarcolemma, sarcoplasm and sarcoplasmic reticulum.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back:
• Sarcolemma = the muscle cell plasma membrane
  • sarcoplasm = its cytoplasm
  • sarcoplasmic reticulum = smooth ER that stores and releases Ca2+.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: On a slide, what three features identify skeletal muscle?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back:
• Striations present
  • long unbranched cylindrical fibres
  • and multiple nuclei pushed to the periphery of the fibre.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What single feature is the give-away for cardiac muscle?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Intercalated discs — dark transverse lines between branched, centrally-nucleated striated cells.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: How do you recognise smooth muscle histologically?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: No striations (uniform pink), fusiform/spindle-shaped cells, each with a single central 'cigar-shaped' nucleus.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Nuclei position/number: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back:
• Skeletal = many, peripheral
  • cardiac = 1–2, central
  • smooth = one, central.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Which muscle types are striated and why do they look striated?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Skeletal and cardiac. Striations come from the regular register of sarcomeres (ordered thick/thin filaments) across myofibrils; smooth muscle lacks this order.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What is a sarcomere and what are its boundaries?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: The functional/contractile unit of striated muscle, running from one Z line to the next Z line.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What does the A band contain and how does it behave during contraction?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: The full length of thick (myosin) filaments; it is dark and its width does NOT change during contraction.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What does the I band contain and what happens on contraction?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Thin (actin) filaments only (light band), bisected by the Z line; it shortens during contraction.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What is the H zone and the M line?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: H zone = central A-band region of thick filaments with no actin overlap (shortens on contraction); M line = central line anchoring thick filaments.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: State the sliding-filament theory in one line.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Filaments don't shorten — thick and thin filaments slide past each other, so the I band and H zone narrow while the A band stays constant.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Which protein is the Ca2+ sensor in skeletal and cardiac muscle, and what does Ca2+ binding do?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Troponin C; Ca2+ binding shifts tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites, allowing cross-bridge cycling.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: List the connective-tissue wrappings of skeletal muscle from outer to inner.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Epimysium (whole muscle) → perimysium (fascicle) → endomysium (individual fibre).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What is a triad and where is it located in skeletal muscle?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: One T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of SR, located at the A–I junction (two triads per sarcomere).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What cells allow skeletal muscle to regenerate, and how good is this?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Satellite cells (quiescent myogenic stem cells between the sarcolemma and basal lamina); regeneration is limited.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What are the three junctions that make up an intercalated disc, and the role of each?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back:
• Fascia adherens (anchors thin filaments, transmits force)
  • desmosomes (mechanical anchoring)
  • and gap junctions (electrical coupling → functional syncytium).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Why does cardiac muscle behave as a functional syncytium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs electrically couple the cells so the myocardium contracts as a coordinated unit.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Contrast the T-tubule arrangement in cardiac vs skeletal muscle.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back:
• Cardiac = diad (one T-tubule + one SR cisterna) at the Z line
  • skeletal = triad (one T-tubule + two SR cisternae) at the A–I junction.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Why does the heart heal by scar after an MI?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Cardiac myocytes lack satellite cells and essentially cannot regenerate, so injury is repaired by collagenous fibrous scar.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What are Purkinje fibres histologically?
