histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Modified cardiac myocytes — larger, pale and glycogen-rich with few myofibrils — specialised for rapid impulse conduction rather than contraction.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Why does smooth muscle show no striations despite having actin and myosin?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Its contractile filaments are not arranged into ordered sarcomeres; thin filaments attach to dense bodies rather than aligned Z lines.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What are dense bodies in smooth muscle?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Cytoplasmic and membrane-associated anchoring structures containing α-actinin — the Z-line equivalent to which thin filaments attach.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: How is contraction triggered in smooth muscle (no troponin)?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Ca2+ binds calmodulin → activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) → phosphorylates myosin → cross-bridge cycling; slow, sustained, efficient.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Single-unit vs multi-unit smooth muscle — key difference and examples.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Single-unit (visceral): coupled by gap junctions, often spontaneously active, contracts as a sheet (gut, uterus, ureter). Multi-unit: individually innervated, fine graded control (iris, ciliary body, vas deferens, large arteries).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Rank the three muscle types by regenerative capacity.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Smooth (good, cells re-enter mitosis) > skeletal (limited, via satellite cells) > cardiac (essentially none).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What is a motor unit and what neurotransmitter/receptor operates at the skeletal NMJ?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: A motor neuron plus all the muscle fibres it innervates; ACh is released and acts on nicotinic ACh receptors, then broken down by acetylcholinesterase.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Contrast Type I and Type II skeletal muscle fibres.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Type I = slow, oxidative, red (myoglobin/mitochondria-rich, fatigue-resistant, postural). Type II = fast, pale — IIa is intermediate (fatigue-resistant, oxidative-glycolytic) while IIx/IIb are glycolytic and fatigue quickly. Shown with myosin ATPase (and NADH-TR/SDH) histochemistry.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Which immunohistochemical markers identify muscle, and which is lost in Duchenne?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back:
• Desmin marks all muscle
  • α-smooth-muscle actin (SMA) marks smooth muscle
  • MyoD/myogenin (nuclear) mark skeletal muscle/rhabdomyosarcoma (myoglobin is a weaker, less specific marker)
  • dystrophin is absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Which stain classically demonstrates cross-striations and intercalated discs?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: PTAH (phosphotungstic acid haematoxylin), which stains them blue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: How does the pregnant uterus enlarge, and how does this differ from a hypertrophied left ventricle?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Smooth muscle enlarges by both hypertrophy AND hyperplasia (pregnant uterus); cardiac (and skeletal) muscle can only undergo hypertrophy (e.g. LV in hypertension).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Name the benign and malignant smooth-muscle tumours and a common example.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Benign = leiomyoma (uterine fibroid is the classic example); malignant = leiomyosarcoma; both are SMA/desmin positive.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What is rhabdomyosarcoma and how is it identified?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: A malignant skeletal-muscle tumour, most common in children; positive for desmin and myogenin (and myoglobin).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: How does excitation–contraction coupling differ mechanistically between skeletal and cardiac muscle?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Skeletal: the T-tubule voltage sensor (DHPR / L-type channel) is MECHANICALLY linked to RyR1 on the SR, so depolarisation physically opens RyR1 — needing little extracellular Ca2+. Cardiac: Ca2+ entering through DHPR triggers Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release via RyR2 — extracellular Ca2+ is required.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What are titin and nebulin?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Titin is the largest protein in the body — an elastic Z-line-to-M-line spring giving passive tension and keeping the thick filament centred; nebulin is an inextensible thin-filament 'ruler' that sets actin filament length.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Outline the cross-bridge cycle and explain rigor mortis.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: ATP binds myosin → head detaches from actin → ATP hydrolysis cocks the head → head binds actin → power stroke (Pi then ADP released) → rigor state until new ATP binds. In rigor mortis, ATP is depleted after death so myosin stays locked to actin, causing stiffness (onset ~2–6 h).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: What is malignant hyperthermia and how is it treated?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: An autosomal-dominant RYR1 (ryanodine receptor) defect in which volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium trigger uncontrolled SR Ca2+ release → muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, rising EtCO₂, tachycardia and rhabdomyolysis; treated by stopping the trigger, cooling and dantrolene (blocks RyR1).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Contrast myasthenia gravis with Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back: Myasthenia gravis: post-synaptic anti-nicotinic-AChR antibodies (associated with thymoma), fatigable weakness that worsens with use, decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation. Lambert–Eaton: pre-synaptic anti-VGCC antibodies (paraneoplastic, small-cell lung cancer), weakness that improves with use, increment on repetitive stimulation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.front: Give the key clinical features of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.back:
X-linked recessive (dystrophin gene, Xp21) affecting boys from ~3–5 yr:
  • proximal weakness with Gower's sign
  • calf pseudohypertrophy
  • markedly raised CK
  • and death from dilated cardiomyopathy/respiratory failure.
Becker is a milder, in-frame variant with reduced (not absent) dystrophin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What are the two cell classes of nervous tissue and their basic roles?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Neurons (excitable, signalling cells that generate and conduct impulses) and neuroglia (supporting cells providing insulation, metabolic/structural support, immune defence and ionic buffering).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: From which germ layer do neurons and most glia arise, and which glial cell is the exception?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Most arise from neuroectoderm (neural tube → CNS; neural crest → PNS neurons, Schwann and satellite cells). Microglia are the exception — they come from mesoderm (monocyte/macrophage lineage).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: How do you recognise a neuron cell body on H&E?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: A large cell with a pale (euchromatic, 'vesicular') nucleus, a single prominent nucleolus, and basophilic Nissl substance ('tigroid') in the cytoplasm.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What is neuropil?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The pink, felt-like background of interwoven dendrites, axons and glial processes seen between neuron cell bodies in grey matter.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Why is white matter pale and what does it contain?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: It is pale because of lipid-rich myelin; it contains myelinated axon tracts and glia with few or no neuron cell bodies.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Where is grey matter located in the brain versus the spinal cord?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: In the brain grey matter is peripheral (cortex) with deep nuclei; in the spinal cord it is central, forming the H/butterfly shape, with white matter outside.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What is Nissl substance and where within the neuron is it found?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Rough ER plus free ribosomes (basophilic); found in the soma and dendrites but NOT in the axon or axon hillock.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What is the axon hillock and why is it important?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The cone-shaped region of the soma where the axon originates; it lacks Nissl substance and is the site of action-potential initiation (initial segment).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Contrast dendrites and axons.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Dendrites are multiple, tapering, branched receptive processes that contain Nissl and often bear spines; the axon is single, uniform in calibre, conducts away from the soma, and has no Nissl.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Describe anterograde vs retrograde axonal transport, including motors.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Anterograde (kinesin) moves organelles/vesicles from soma to terminal; retrograde (dynein) moves material from terminal to soma — the latter is also exploited by rabies, tetanus toxin and herpes virus.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Classify neurons by number of processes, with an example of each.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back:
• Multipolar (1 axon + many dendrites; motor neurons/interneurons — commonest)
  • bipolar (1 axon + 1 dendrite; retina, olfactory, vestibulocochlear)
  • pseudounipolar (single process that splits; dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons)
  • unipolar (one process; mainly invertebrate/embryonic).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Name the two neuronal pigments and their significance.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back:
• Lipofuscin — yellow-brown lysosomal 'wear-and-tear' pigment that accumulates with age
  • neuromelanin — dark pigment in substantia nigra and locus coeruleus neurons, whose loss (nigral pallor) is the gross hallmark of Parkinson's disease.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Classify neurons by function.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back:
• Sensory (afferent, toward CNS)
  • motor (efferent, away from CNS)
  • and interneurons (connect the two; the majority of CNS neurons).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Which is the most abundant glial cell and what are its key functions?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back:
The astrocyte —
  • structural/metabolic support
  • K+ and neurotransmitter buffering
  • inducing and maintaining the blood–brain barrier via end-feet (the barrier proper is endothelial tight junctions)
  • and the glial scar.
Marker: GFAP.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Distinguish fibrous and protoplasmic astrocytes.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Fibrous astrocytes are found in white matter (long, thin processes); protoplasmic astrocytes are in grey matter (shorter, bushier processes).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Which cell myelinates CNS axons and how many can one cell myelinate?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The oligodendrocyte; one oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of several (up to ~50) axons.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What are microglia and where do they come from?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm (monocyte lineage); they perform immune surveillance and phagocytosis.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What are ependymal cells and where are they found?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Ciliated cuboidal/columnar cells lining the ventricles and central canal; they help circulate CSF and are specialised as choroid plexus to produce CSF.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Which cell myelinates PNS axons and what is the one-cell rule?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The Schwann cell; one Schwann cell forms exactly one internode of myelin (and can also ensheath several unmyelinated axons). Marker: S100.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What are satellite cells?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Glial cells that surround neuron cell bodies within peripheral ganglia and regulate their microenvironment.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What are nodes of Ranvier and what do they contain?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Periodic gaps in the myelin sheath that are densely packed with voltage-gated Na+ channels.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Define saltatory conduction and why it is advantageous.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The action potential 'jumps' from node to node along a myelinated axon, giving faster and more metabolically efficient conduction than continuous conduction in unmyelinated fibres.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What is the neurilemma and why does it matter for regeneration?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The Schwann-cell cytoplasm plus basal lamina surrounding a PNS fibre; it forms a guiding tube that allows peripheral axon regeneration — CNS axons lack it and regenerate poorly.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: List the connective-tissue coverings of a peripheral nerve from inner to outer.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Endoneurium (around each axon/Schwann unit) → perineurium (around each fascicle) → epineurium (around the whole nerve).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Which nerve covering forms the blood–nerve barrier?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The perineurium (its specialised epithelioid cells).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Contrast dorsal root ganglion and autonomic ganglion histology.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Dorsal root ganglion: pseudounipolar cell bodies arranged in ordered rows, ringed by satellite cells. Autonomic ganglion: scattered multipolar cell bodies with eccentric nuclei.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Describe the components of a chemical synapse.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: A presynaptic terminal with neurotransmitter vesicles and mitochondria, a synaptic cleft (~20–40 nm), and a postsynaptic density bearing receptors; Ca2+ entry triggers vesicle fusion and unidirectional transmitter release.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: How does an electrical synapse differ from a chemical one?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Electrical synapses use gap junctions for direct ionic current flow — very fast and bidirectional — whereas chemical synapses use neurotransmitter and are unidirectional with a synaptic delay.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Name the three synapse types by site.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Axo-dendritic (commonest), axo-somatic and axo-axonic.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Which stain highlights neuron cell bodies by staining Nissl substance?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: The Nissl stain (cresyl violet or toluidine blue).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Which stain is used to demonstrate myelin?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Luxol fast blue (myelin blue); osmium tetroxide also blackens myelin lipid.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Match the IHC markers: GFAP, S100, NeuN, synaptophysin.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back:
• GFAP = astrocytes
  • S100 = Schwann cells (and melanocytes)
  • NeuN = neuronal nuclei
  • synaptophysin = synaptic vesicles/synapses.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Contrast the demyelinating targets in multiple sclerosis and Guillain–Barré syndrome.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Multiple sclerosis is CNS demyelination (oligodendrocyte target); Guillain–Barré is usually PNS demyelination (AIDP; Schwann cell/root target), though an axonal variant (AMAN, anti-GM1, post-Campylobacter) also occurs.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What is chromatolysis and when is it seen?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Following axonal injury the Nissl substance disperses, the soma swells and the nucleus moves to the periphery — a reversible repair response of the cell body.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Why do most primary brain tumours arise from glia rather than neurons?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Mature neurons are post-mitotic and rarely divide, whereas glial cells retain proliferative capacity — so gliomas (astrocytoma/glioblastoma) are the commonest primary MALIGNANT CNS tumours (though metastases and meningiomas are commoner overall).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Distinguish the blood–brain barrier from the blood–CSF barrier.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Blood–brain barrier = tight-junctioned capillary endothelium (induced/maintained by astrocyte end-feet). Blood–CSF barrier = tight junctions between choroid plexus epithelial cells — the plexus capillaries themselves are fenestrated.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Define mesaxon, Schmidt–Lanterman incisures and a Remak bundle.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back:
• Mesaxon = the paired Schwann-cell membrane that spirals to form PNS myelin
  • Schmidt–Lanterman incisures = pockets of retained Schwann cytoplasm within the myelin sheath
  • Remak bundle = several unmyelinated axons ensheathed in the troughs of a single Schwann cell.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: Outline Wallerian degeneration and the PNS regeneration rate.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: After axon transection the distal axon and its myelin fragment (24–72 h) and are cleared by macrophages and Schwann cells; Schwann cells proliferate into bands of Büngner that guide regrowth at ~1 mm/day. CNS axons fail — glial scar plus myelin inhibitors (Nogo, MAG).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.front: What are schwannomas and neurofibromas, and which marker identifies them?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue.back: Benign peripheral nerve-sheath tumours that are S100-positive; a vestibular schwannoma ('acoustic neuroma') arises at the cerebellopontine angle, and these tumours are associated with neurofibromatosis (NF1/NF2).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Which fixative is used for routine (paraffin) histological processing?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: 10% neutral-buffered formalin is the routine fixative — it cross-links proteins to halt autolysis/decay and hardens tissue. Ethanol and xylene are dehydration/clearing agents, not the primary fixative; glutaraldehyde is used for electron microscopy; liquid nitrogen is for frozen sections.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: During tissue processing, what is the role of xylene?
options: It clears the alcohol so paraffin wax can infiltrate
It removes water from the tissue
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Xylene is the clearing agent — after graded alcohols dehydrate the tissue, xylene removes the alcohol so molten paraffin wax can infiltrate. Fixation is by formalin; nuclear staining is haematoxylin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A surgeon needs to know intra-operatively whether a tumour margin is clear. Which technique gives an answer within minutes?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: A frozen section (snap-freeze + cryostat) skips wax processing and delivers a diagnosis in minutes, making it ideal for intra-operative margin assessment. Routine paraffin processing takes far longer; IHC and EM are slower still.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Why can lipids only be demonstrated on frozen (not paraffin) sections?
options: The organic solvents used in wax processing dissolve fat
Lipids are too small to see by light microscopy
Lipids do not take up any stain
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Routine processing uses alcohols and xylene, which dissolve fat — so lipids are lost from paraffin sections. Frozen tissue avoids solvents, so Oil Red O or Sudan can stain lipid red.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: On an H&E section, which structure stains blue with haematoxylin?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Haematoxylin is a basic dye that binds acidic (basophilic) structures — above all the nucleus (DNA), plus RER/ribosomes. Collagen, cytoplasm, RBCs and keratin are eosinophilic and stain pink with eosin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A plasma cell shows strongly basophilic (blue) cytoplasm. What does this indicate?
options: Abundant rough ER/ribosomes for protein synthesis
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Basophilic cytoplasm reflects abundant rough ER and ribosomes (RNA is acidic and binds haematoxylin) — the hallmark of a cell actively synthesising protein, such as a plasma cell or pancreatic acinar cell.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A renal biopsy is stained to assess basement membranes and shows them in magenta; adding diastase does not remove the colour. Which stain was used?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: PAS stains basement membranes, glycogen, mucin and fungi magenta. Diastase digests glycogen: because the basement-membrane staining persists after diastase, it is not glycogen. Trichrome shows collagen; Congo red shows amyloid; ZN shows acid-fast bacilli.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Amyloid is suspected in a renal biopsy. Which stain confirms it, and what is the diagnostic feature?
options: Congo red — apple-green birefringence under polarised light
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Congo red stains amyloid, which then shows characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarised light — the diagnostic finding. The other stains target glycogen/BM, iron, lipid and reticular fibres respectively.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A caseating granuloma is stained to look for the causative organism, which appears as red rods on a blue background. Which stain and organism?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Ziehl–Neelsen demonstrates acid-fast bacilli as red rods on a blue counterstain — classic for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Giemsa is used for H. pylori/blood films; PAS for fungi.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A liver biopsy is stained to grade fibrosis, with collagen appearing blue/green and muscle/cytoplasm red. Which stain is this?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Masson's trichrome distinguishes collagen (blue/green) from muscle/cytoplasm (red) and is used to grade fibrosis such as in cirrhosis. Elastic stains show elastic fibres black; Perls' shows iron.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Which stain would best demonstrate haemosiderin (iron) deposition?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Perls' Prussian blue turns ferric iron/haemosiderin blue — used in haemochromatosis and old haemorrhage. The others target amyloid, lipid, acid-fast bacilli and reticular fibres.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Immunohistochemistry on a poorly-differentiated tumour is strongly positive for cytokeratin. What does this indicate?
options: It is of epithelial origin (a carcinoma)
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Cytokeratins mark epithelial cells, so cytokeratin positivity indicates a carcinoma. CD45 would suggest lymphoma, S100 melanoma/nerve, and vimentin a mesenchymal/sarcomatous tumour.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Which immunohistochemical panel is used to classify a breast cancer and guide treatment?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 status classify breast cancer and direct therapy (e.g. HER2-positive tumours are treated with trastuzumab). Ki-67 adds a proliferation index but is not the defining panel.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: What is the correct first step when examining an unknown slide?
options: Go straight to high power to identify cells
Start at low power to assess architecture and orientation
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Always read low power first — assess capsule and overall architecture (tube, lobules, follicles, tubules) to orient and guess the organ — then move to medium and high power. Architecture before cytology.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: The total magnification of a light microscope is calculated as:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Total magnification = objective × eyepiece (e.g. 40× × 10× = 400×). Useful light magnification reaches ~1000×, limited by a resolution of ~0.2 µm set by the wavelength of light.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A child has recurrent chest infections and situs inversus; primary ciliary dyskinesia is suspected. Which modality confirms the ciliary defect?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Electron microscopy is needed to see the cilia axoneme and its dynein arms — absent/defective dynein arms confirm primary ciliary dyskinesia. Light microscopy (~0.2 µm resolution) cannot resolve axonemal ultrastructure.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A trainee reports a 'lesion' that is a perfectly straight, empty cleft running across the section, partly off the tissue edge. What is the most likely explanation?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: A perfectly straight, empty cleft is a classic sectioning/processing artefact (a fold, tear or knife mark) rather than pathology — geometric regularity and location partly off the tissue are the clues.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Which histological feature is eosinophilic (stains pink with eosin)?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Eosin is acidic and binds basic (eosinophilic) structures — cytoplasmic proteins, collagen, muscle, RBCs and keratin (pink). Chromatin, ribosomes, nucleolus and DNA are basophilic and stain blue with haematoxylin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A dye stains mast-cell granules purple rather than its own blue colour. This property is called:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Metachromasia is when a dye colours a component differently from the dye itself; toluidine blue shows this with mast cells and cartilage GAGs (purple).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Immunofluorescence differs from standard immunohistochemistry in that it uses:
options: A fluorescent label viewed under a fluorescence microscope
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Immunofluorescence tags the antibody with a fluorophore (viewed under UV/fluorescence microscopy), commonly on renal and skin biopsies; standard IHC uses an enzyme/chromogen visible by light microscopy.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Which stain would you add to demonstrate fungi if PAS were equivocal?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: GMS silver stains fungal cell walls black and is a standard alternative/adjunct to PAS for fungi.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Graded alcohols (increasing strength) are used during dehydration to:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: A stepwise increase in alcohol concentration dehydrates gently, minimising the shrinkage and distortion that immediate absolute alcohol would cause.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A frozen section is fast primarily because it:
options: Skips fixation and paraffin processing (tissue is frozen and cut on a cryostat)
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Freezing tissue in OCT and cutting on a cryostat avoids the lengthy fixation/dehydration/embedding steps, giving an intra-operative answer in minutes.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Auramine–rhodamine staining is used to detect:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Auramine–rhodamine is a fluorescent stain for acid-fast bacilli, an alternative to Ziehl–Neelsen for mycobacteria such as TB.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Which stain best demonstrates the acidic goblet-cell mucin of intestinal metaplasia in Barrett's oesophagus?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Alcian blue stains acidic mucins blue; AB–PAS distinguishes acidic (blue) from neutral (magenta) mucins, demonstrating goblet cells in Barrett's.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: A silver (Grocott/GMS) stain of lung from an immunocompromised patient shows black cup-shaped cysts. The organism is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: GMS blackens Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts (classic cup/helmet shape) causing PCP in the immunocompromised.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.question: Which stain highlights the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans rose-red?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of.explanation: Mucicarmine stains mucin (and the mucopolysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus) rose-red; it also marks adenocarcinoma mucin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Which of the following provides bone with its compressive strength and acts as the body's mineral reservoir?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Inorganic hydroxyapatite [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2] gives compressive strength/hardness and stores ~99% of body calcium. Type I collagen provides tensile strength/flexibility; osteocalcin is a matrix protein; elastin is not a major bone component.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: The concentric lamellae arranged around a central neurovascular canal in compact bone form which structure?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: An osteon (Haversian system) is the structural unit of compact bone — concentric lamellae around a central Haversian canal. Trabeculae make up cancellous bone (no osteons); lacunae house osteocytes.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: How do Volkmann's canals differ from Haversian canals?
options: They are found only in cancellous bone
They contain only nerves, no vessels
They run transversely, connecting Haversian canals and the periosteum
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Volkmann's (perforating) canals run transversely and connect Haversian canals to each other and to the periosteum, whereas Haversian canals run longitudinally within osteons. Both carry neurovascular bundles.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Why does cancellous (trabecular) bone lack osteons?
options: It is made only of cartilage
Its trabeculae are thin and nourished by diffusion from marrow, so no central canal is needed
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Trabeculae are thin enough to be supplied by diffusion from the adjacent marrow, so they do not need the central vascular canal of an osteon. Cancellous bone still contains osteocytes and collagen.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: A large multinucleated cell is seen resorbing bone within a Howship's lacuna. From which cell lineage does it arise?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: The osteoclast is the bone-resorbing cell and is the only bone cell of haematopoietic (monocyte/macrophage) origin. Osteoprogenitors, osteoblasts and osteocytes are all mesenchymal.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Which enzyme, secreted across the osteoclast's ruffled border, digests the organic (collagen) matrix of bone?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: The osteoclast secretes H+ (dissolving mineral) and cathepsin K (digesting type I collagen) across its ruffled border into Howship's lacuna. Alkaline phosphatase is an osteoblast marker of bone formation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: On a decalcified H&E section, which appearance best identifies an osteoblast?
options: A cuboidal cell with basophilic cytoplasm lining a bone surface, laying down osteoid
A large multinucleated cell in a resorption bay
A cell with a ruffled border
A flat cell trapped in a lacuna
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteoblasts are cuboidal with basophilic cytoplasm (abundant RER) and line bone surfaces, secreting osteoid. The multinucleated cell in a resorption bay is an osteoclast; the cell trapped in a lacuna is an osteocyte.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Osteoblasts drive osteoclast formation by expressing which molecule, the target of the drug denosumab?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteoblasts express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to promote resorption; denosumab is a monoclonal anti-RANKL antibody. OPG is the endogenous decoy that blocks RANKL.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: In a ground (undecalcified) bone section, the lacunae and canaliculi appear black. Why?
options: The cells are lost and the spaces fill with air/debris that block light
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: In a ground section the cells are lost and the empty lacunae/canaliculi fill with air and debris, which appear black under transmitted light — this beautifully outlines osteon architecture.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Which bones form by intramembranous ossification (directly from mesenchyme, without a cartilage model)?
options: The flat bones of the skull vault, clavicle and mandible
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly from mesenchyme and produces the flat bones — skull vault, most facial bones, clavicle and mandible. Long bones, vertebrae and skull base form by endochondral ossification (cartilage model).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Longitudinal growth of a long bone occurs at the epiphyseal plate. Which is the correct order of its zones from the epiphysis toward the diaphysis?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: From the epiphysis down: Resting/reserve → Proliferation (chondrocytes stack) → Hypertrophy → Calcification → Ossification (osteoblasts lay bone on calcified cartilage). The plate fuses after puberty, ending longitudinal growth.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: A post-menopausal woman sustains a fragility fracture. Bone histology would most likely show:
options: Dense bone with no marrow space
Reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation
A mosaic pattern of cement lines
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Post-menopausal osteoporosis = reduced bone MASS with normal mineralisation (oestrogen loss → resorption > formation). Excess osteoid indicates osteomalacia; mosaic cement lines indicate Paget's; dense marrow-crowded bone indicates osteopetrosis.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: A patient with vitamin D deficiency has bone pain. A Goldner's trichrome stain shows wide red seams of unmineralised matrix. What is the diagnosis?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteomalacia is defective mineralisation with accumulation of unmineralised osteoid (red on Goldner's trichrome), typically from vitamin D deficiency. Osteoporosis shows reduced mass but normal mineralisation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Which hormone increases bone resorption indirectly (via osteoblast RANKL) and raises serum calcium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: PTH raises serum calcium partly by stimulating osteoblasts to express RANKL, increasing osteoclastic resorption. Calcitonin does the opposite (inhibits osteoclasts); oestrogen restrains resorption.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: A child has multiple fractures and blue sclerae; a defect in type I collagen is found. What is the diagnosis?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta results from a type I collagen mutation → brittle bones and blue sclerae. Osteopetrosis is due to osteoclast dysfunction; rickets is defective mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Dense, brittle bones with obliteration of the marrow cavity and a tendency to fracture describes:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteopetrosis (marble bone disease) is caused by osteoclast dysfunction — bone is not resorbed, so it becomes dense but brittle and crowds out the marrow. The others involve reduced mass, poor mineralisation, collagen defect, or excess resorption.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: What is the correct sequence of fracture healing?
options: Haematoma → soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus → hard (woven bone) callus → remodelling to lamellar bone
Soft callus → haematoma → remodelling → hard callus
Haematoma → hard callus → soft callus → remodelling
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Fracture healing proceeds: haematoma → soft fibrocartilaginous callus → hard woven-bone callus → remodelling to mature lamellar bone — recapitulating endochondral development.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Which statement about the osteocyte is correct?
options: It lines the marrow cavity as endosteum
It sits in a lacuna and acts as a mechanosensor directing remodelling
It is multinucleated and resorbs bone
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: The osteocyte is a mature osteoblast trapped in a lacuna, communicating via canaliculi; it maintains matrix and acts as the principal mechanosensor that orchestrates remodelling. Osteoid secretion is by surface osteoblasts; resorption is by osteoclasts.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Before routine paraffin sectioning, bone must be:
options: Decalcified (or cut as a ground section)
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: The mineral makes bone too hard to cut, so it must be decalcified (e.g. EDTA/acid) to allow microtomy, or prepared as a thin ground (undecalcified) section. Decalcified H&E preserves cells; ground sections show osteon architecture.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Osteocyte processes communicate with each other through:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Canaliculi are the fine channels connecting lacunae; osteocyte cytoplasmic processes run through them, allowing communication and diffusion of nutrients.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Alkaline phosphatase in serum is a marker of:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Alkaline phosphatase is produced by active osteoblasts and rises with bone formation (e.g. Paget's disease, healing fracture, growth).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism develops bone lesions with fibrous replacement and 'brown tumours'. This is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Excess PTH drives osteoclastic resorption, replacing bone with fibrous tissue and forming brown tumours — osteitis fibrosa cystica.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: In a long bone, the region immediately adjacent to the growth plate is the:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: The metaphysis lies between the epiphysis and diaphysis, adjacent to the epiphyseal (growth) plate where longitudinal growth occurs.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Osteoblasts secrete osteoid, which is:
options: The unmineralised organic matrix (mainly type I collagen)
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteoid is the newly secreted unmineralised organic matrix; hydroxyapatite is subsequently deposited to mineralise it. Excess unmineralised osteoid indicates osteomalacia.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: A patient has a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase but normal serum calcium, phosphate and PTH. The most likely diagnosis is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Paget's disease shows a very high (often isolated) ALP from rapid bone turnover, with normal calcium and phosphate. Osteoporosis is all-normal; primary hyperPTH raises Ca and lowers PO4; osteomalacia lowers Ca/PO4 and raises ALP and PTH.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: A 15-year-old has a painful mass at the distal femoral metaphysis; X-ray shows a sunburst pattern and a Codman triangle. The most likely diagnosis is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary bone malignancy in adolescents, arising at the metaphysis of long bones (distal femur/proximal tibia) with a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle; it also occurs in the elderly with Paget's.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Which osteocyte-derived protein inhibits Wnt signalling to suppress bone formation and is the target of romosozumab?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Osteocytes secrete sclerostin (SOST), which inhibits Wnt signalling in osteoblasts → less bone formation; mechanical loading lowers it. Romosozumab is an anti-sclerostin anabolic agent.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.question: Alendronate reduces bone resorption chiefly by:
options: Binding hydroxyapatite and inhibiting osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase → osteoclast apoptosis
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact,.explanation: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates bind hydroxyapatite, are taken up by osteoclasts and inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, causing osteoclast apoptosis; denosumab (not a bisphosphonate) blocks RANKL.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Blood is classified as which type of tissue?
options: A type of epithelium lining vessels
A connective tissue with a fluid (liquid) matrix
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Blood is a specialised connective tissue whose matrix — plasma — is liquid. Cells (formed elements) are suspended in this fluid matrix.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: What is serum?
options: Plasma minus the clotting factors (after clotting)
Plasma with the cells still in it
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Serum is what remains after blood has clotted — plasma minus fibrinogen and the other consumed clotting factors.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: After centrifugation, the thin buffy coat between plasma and packed red cells contains:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: The buffy coat is the thin middle layer of white cells and platelets; red cells pack at the bottom (the haematocrit fraction) and plasma sits on top.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Which stain is routinely used to examine a peripheral blood film?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Blood films are stained with Romanowsky stains (Giemsa, Wright or Leishman), combining acidic eosin and basic methylene blue. H&E is for tissue sections, not films.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: The central pallor of a normal red blood cell is explained by:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Red cells are biconcave, so the centre is thinner and appears pale; the disc shape also maximises surface-area:volume for gas exchange. Mature red cells have no nucleus.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: A normal red blood cell measures approximately:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: A red cell is ~7–8 µm — small enough to use as a 'ruler' on the film for sizing white cells and judging red-cell size (micro- vs macrocytic).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: A blood film shows faintly blue-tinged larger red cells (polychromasia); a supravital stain reveals a reticular network. These are:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Reticulocytes are young red cells with residual ribosomal RNA — bluish (polychromatic) on a routine film, with a reticular network on supravital staining. A raised count indicates active marrow output.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Which is the most numerous white cell in normal adult blood, and its main role?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Neutrophils are the commonest WBC (40–75%) and are the front-line phagocytes of acute bacterial infection. Frequency order: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Which leukocyte is the largest and has a kidney/horseshoe-shaped nucleus, becoming a macrophage in tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: The monocyte is the largest WBC, with an eccentric horseshoe/kidney-shaped nucleus and abundant grey-blue cytoplasm; in tissue it differentiates into macrophages and dendritic cells.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: A patient with asthma and a worm infection has a raised count of a cell with a bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules. Which cell?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Eosinophils (bilobed nucleus, red-orange granules) are raised in parasitic infection and allergy/type I hypersensitivity such as asthma.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 nuclear lobes) on a film point to which deficiency?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Hypersegmented neutrophils are a classic clue to B12/folate (megaloblastic) deficiency. Iron deficiency causes microcytic — not megaloblastic — changes.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Platelets are best described as:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Platelets are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments shed by megakaryocytes in the marrow; they drive haemostasis and provide a phospholipid surface for coagulation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: In a healthy adult, haemopoiesis normally occurs in the:
options: Red bone marrow (axial skeleton, pelvis, proximal long bones)
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: After birth, blood cells are made in red bone marrow — in adults chiefly the axial skeleton, pelvis and proximal femur/humerus. Liver/spleen are the fetal sites (and can restart as extramedullary haemopoiesis).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: During fetal life, the main site of blood cell production is the:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Haemopoiesis shifts yolk sac (embryo) → liver and spleen (fetus) → red bone marrow (postnatal).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Erythropoietin, which drives red-cell production, is secreted by the ______ in response to ______.
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: The kidney senses tissue hypoxia and releases erythropoietin (EPO), stimulating erythropoiesis. TPO drives platelets and G-CSF drives neutrophils.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Which event marks the transition to a reticulocyte during erythropoiesis?
options: Extrusion of the nucleus from the orthochromatic erythroblast
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: The orthochromatic erythroblast (normoblast) extrudes its nucleus to become a reticulocyte, which still contains residual RNA before maturing into a red cell.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: A patient presents with fatigue, bruising and infections; the film shows numerous circulating blast cells. This most likely indicates:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Circulating blasts on a peripheral film suggest acute leukaemia, which — with pancytopenic symptoms (fatigue, bruising, infection) — is a haematological emergency requiring urgent referral.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Which description best fits a lymphocyte?
options: Large cell with a horseshoe nucleus and grey-blue cytoplasm
Small cell with a large round dense nucleus and a thin rim of pale-blue cytoplasm
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: A lymphocyte has a large, round, dense (heterochromatic) nucleus filling most of the cell, with only a thin rim of pale-blue cytoplasm; it mediates adaptive immunity (B, T, NK).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: The haematocrit represents the:
options: Fraction of blood volume that is red cells
Percentage of white cells in blood
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Haematocrit is the proportion of blood volume made up of packed red cells (~40–54% in men), read off centrifuged blood below the buffy coat.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: An increased number of band (non-segmented) neutrophils on a film indicates:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Bands are immature neutrophils; a rise ('left shift') reflects increased marrow output in acute bacterial infection/inflammation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Platelets are produced by which marrow cell?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: The megakaryocyte is a large polyploid cell whose cytoplasm fragments into platelets, a process driven by thrombopoietin.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Which term describes variation in the SHAPE of red blood cells?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Poikilocytosis is variation in red-cell shape; anisocytosis is variation in size. Both are non-specific features of many anaemias.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Haemoglobin is best described as:
options: An iron-containing tetramer of globin chains that binds oxygen
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Haemoglobin is a tetramer (2α + 2β globin, each with a haem/iron group) that reversibly binds oxygen; it fills red cells and is responsible for their pink staining.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Antibody production is the specific role of which cell?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: B lymphocytes differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells; T lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity and NK cells provide innate cytotoxicity.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: A blood film shows red cells containing small round basophilic nuclear remnants (Howell–Jolly bodies). This indicates:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Howell–Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants normally pitted out by the spleen; seeing them implies hyposplenism or previous splenectomy.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Numerous red-cell fragments (schistocytes) with thrombocytopenia in a septic patient most suggest:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Schistocytes are mechanically sheared red cells seen in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — DIC, TTP/HUS or mechanical valves.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: A bone-marrow blast containing a needle-like azurophilic (Auer) rod is diagnostic of:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Auer rods are crystallised azurophilic granules found in myeloblasts, diagnostic of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: Marked rouleaux formation on a film, with a very high ESR and back pain, points to:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Rouleaux (coin-stacking) reflects a high plasma paraprotein/fibrinogen, classically multiple myeloma, which also raises the ESR.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.question: A film from an elderly patient shows a lymphocytosis with many fragile 'smudge' (smear) cells. The likely diagnosis is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemop.explanation: Smudge/smear cells are fragile lymphocytes ruptured during smearing, characteristic of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Cartilage is avascular. How are its chondrocytes supplied with nutrients?
options: By a rich capillary network in the lacunae
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Cartilage has no blood vessels; chondrocytes are nourished by diffusion through the matrix (and from the perichondrium where present). This is why cartilage heals slowly.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Which collagen type predominates in hyaline and elastic cartilage?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Hyaline and elastic cartilage are built on type II collagen. Fibrocartilage instead uses type I collagen in visible bundles.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Which matrix component gives cartilage its ability to resist compression?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: The hydrated proteoglycan–GAG gel (aggrecan, chondroitin/keratan sulfate) resists compression; collagen resists tension. Hydroxyapatite is a bone, not cartilage, component.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: A cluster of 2–4 chondrocytes within a shared region of matrix is called:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Isogenous groups (cell nests) are clusters of chondrocytes derived from a single dividing cell — the hallmark of interstitial growth.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Appositional growth of cartilage arises from which structure?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Appositional (surface) growth adds new cartilage from the chondrogenic layer of the perichondrium; interstitial growth is by chondrocytes dividing within the matrix.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Which cartilage type is found in the trachea, costal cartilage and articular surfaces?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Hyaline cartilage — the commonest type — lines articular surfaces and forms costal cartilage, the tracheal rings, larynx and nose, plus the growth plate and fetal skeleton.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: A biopsy of the external ear (pinna) would show which cartilage, identifiable by which special feature?
options: Elastic cartilage; a network of elastic fibres
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: The pinna is elastic cartilage, characterised by an abundant network of elastic fibres (shown with an elastic stain) that give it flexible recoil. The epiglottis and auditory tube are also elastic.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: A patient has an intervertebral disc that must resist both compression and strong tensile/shear forces. The annulus fibrosus is made of which cartilage?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Fibrocartilage (type I collagen, no perichondrium) combines tensile strength with compression resistance — ideal for intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis and knee menisci.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Which cartilage lacks a perichondrium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Fibrocartilage and articular hyaline cartilage have no perichondrium; most other hyaline and all elastic cartilage do.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Which stain demonstrates cartilage GAGs by metachromasia (staining them purple)?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Toluidine (or methylene) blue produces metachromasia — the sulfated GAGs stain purple rather than blue. Alcian blue and safranin O also mark cartilage proteoglycans.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Why does hyaline cartilage appear glassy and homogeneous on H&E, with collagen not visible?
options: Collagen is only in the perichondrium
Type II collagen has the same refractive index as the ground substance, so it is masked
The collagen is dissolved during processing
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Type II collagen fibrils are fine and share the refractive index of the surrounding ground substance, so they are 'masked' — giving hyaline its glassy homogeneous appearance.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: In osteoarthritis, the primary tissue change is:
options: Progressive loss of articular hyaline cartilage with proteoglycan depletion
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Osteoarthritis is characterised by progressive erosion of articular hyaline cartilage with proteoglycan loss; because cartilage is avascular, repair is poor.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Which mutation causes achondroplasia by disrupting the hyaline growth plate?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Achondroplasia results from an FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation (autosomal dominant) that impairs chondrocyte proliferation in the hyaline growth plate (endochondral ossification), producing short-limb dwarfism. COL1A1 defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta; FBN1 causes Marfan syndrome.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: A young chondrocyte divides within the matrix, forming isogenous groups and enlarging the cartilage from within. This is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Growth from within, by chondrocytes dividing inside the matrix to form isogenous groups, is interstitial growth (prominent in young cartilage and the growth plate). Appositional growth adds cartilage from the perichondrium.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: A patient presents with painful, floppy, red ears, a saddle-nose deformity and airway problems from cartilage inflammation. The likely diagnosis is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Relapsing polychondritis is an autoimmune attack on cartilage producing inflamed floppy ears, saddle-nose and airway collapse.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: The rim of darker, GAG-rich matrix immediately around a chondrocyte lacuna is the:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: The territorial (capsular) matrix is the more basophilic zone hugging each lacuna; the interterritorial matrix lies between the cell groups.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Articular cartilage differs from most hyaline cartilage in that it:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Articular cartilage has no perichondrium (its surface must articulate), which — with its avascularity — gives it very poor repair capacity.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Once articular cartilage is fully lost in advanced osteoarthritis, the exposed subchondral bone becomes polished and ivory-like. This is termed:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Eburnation is the polished, ivory-like appearance of subchondral bone rubbing on bone after full-thickness cartilage loss in OA; other features include osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Which cartilage type shows visible thick collagen bundles because it contains type I collagen?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Fibrocartilage contains predominantly type I collagen (with some type II) in thick, visible bundles; hyaline and elastic cartilage use type II collagen, which is masked and glassy on H&E.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray with acute knee arthritis and rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals in the joint fluid indicates:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: CPPD (pseudogout) deposits calcium pyrophosphate in fibrocartilage (menisci) and hyaline cartilage → chondrocalcinosis; crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent, unlike gout's negatively birefringent needles.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: In articular cartilage, the basophilic line separating the deep (radial) zone from the underlying calcified zone is the:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: The tidemark is the basophilic boundary between uncalcified radial cartilage and the calcified zone that anchors articular cartilage to subchondral bone.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Painful, red, swollen ears that characteristically SPARE the ear lobes, with a saddle-nose deformity, suggest:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Relapsing polychondritis inflames cartilage but spares the ear lobe (which is fibrofatty, not cartilage); septal cartilage destruction gives the saddle-nose deformity.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.question: Most long bones develop by which process, using hyaline cartilage as a template?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hya.explanation: Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model with bone and drives long-bone growth at the epiphyseal plate; intramembranous ossification (flat skull bones) uses no cartilage template.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: What best distinguishes connective tissue from epithelium histologically?
options: Connective tissue has sparse cells within an abundant extracellular matrix
Connective tissue has tightly packed cells and no matrix
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Connective tissue is defined by abundant extracellular matrix with relatively few, scattered cells — the opposite of epithelium's densely packed cells with minimal matrix.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which cell is the most numerous in connective tissue and produces its fibres and ground substance?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: The fibroblast is the commonest CT cell and synthesises both the fibres (collagen, elastic, reticular) and the ground substance.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: A cell with a clock-face (cartwheel) nucleus, basophilic cytoplasm and a pale perinuclear hof is a:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: This describes a plasma cell (a differentiated B lymphocyte) that secretes antibody. Its RER-rich cytoplasm is basophilic, and the Golgi produces the perinuclear hof.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Reticular fibres form the framework of organs such as the liver and lymph node. What are they, and how are they best demonstrated?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Reticular fibres are type III collagen; they are invisible on H&E and are shown black by silver (reticulin) staining, outlining organ stroma.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which fibre type provides stretch and recoil and requires a special stain (e.g. Verhoeff) to visualise?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Elastic fibres (elastin + fibrillin) give tissues stretch and recoil (large arteries, some ligaments) and need an elastic stain to be seen on section.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: A tendon is composed of which connective tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Tendons (and ligaments/aponeuroses) are dense regular connective tissue — parallel collagen bundles giving tensile strength in one direction.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: The dermis and organ capsules, which must resist tension from many directions, are made of:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen bundles running in random directions, resisting multidirectional tension — as in the dermis, capsules, submucosa and periosteum.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which connective tissue is the general-purpose 'packing material' found in the lamina propria beneath epithelia?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Loose (areolar) CT — with all fibre types, many cells and abundant ground substance — is the general support/packing tissue, e.g. the lamina propria.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Brown adipose tissue differs from white adipose in that it is:
options: Multilocular with many mitochondria and generates heat via UCP1
A type of dense regular tissue
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Brown fat is multilocular (many small droplets, central nucleus) and mitochondria-rich; it produces heat by UCP1-mediated thermogenesis and is prominent in neonates. White fat is unilocular (signet-ring) for storage.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: A hyperflexible patient with stretchy, fragile skin and easy bruising most likely has a defect in:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome results from defective collagen, producing joint hypermobility and fragile, hyperextensible skin. Fibrillin/elastin defects underlie Marfan syndrome instead.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: A patient with Marfan syndrome develops aortic dilatation. The underlying defect is in:
options: Fibrillin (FBN1), a component of elastic fibres
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Marfan syndrome is caused by an FBN1 (fibrillin) mutation weakening elastic tissue, predisposing to aortic aneurysm/dissection and lens dislocation.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Poor wound healing, perifollicular haemorrhage and bleeding gums due to defective collagen synthesis indicate a deficiency of:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase; deficiency (scurvy) impairs hydroxylation of proline/lysine, so the collagen triple helix cannot stabilise — causing poor healing and bleeding gums. (Cross-linking failure is instead the copper/lysyl-oxidase story.)

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which cell, when it degranulates in type I hypersensitivity, releases histamine to cause allergy and anaphylaxis?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Mast cells store histamine and heparin; their degranulation in type I hypersensitivity drives allergic reactions and anaphylaxis. They show toluidine-blue metachromasia.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: On a routine H&E section, adipocytes appear as empty 'signet-ring' spaces because:
options: The lipid is dissolved out by the solvents used in processing
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Routine processing uses alcohols and xylene, which dissolve the fat, leaving an empty vacuole with the nucleus pushed to the rim. Oil Red O on frozen tissue preserves and stains the lipid.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which stain would you request to grade collagen deposition (fibrosis) in a tissue?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Masson's trichrome stains collagen blue/green and is used to assess/grade fibrosis. Congo red is for amyloid, Perls' for iron, ZN for acid-fast bacilli.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which two mediators are stored in the cytoplasmic granules of mast cells?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Mast-cell granules store histamine (vasoactive) and heparin (anticoagulant); surface IgE cross-linking triggers degranulation in type I hypersensitivity.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Tissue macrophages (Kupffer cells, microglia, osteoclasts, alveolar macrophages) belong to the:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: These monocyte-derived phagocytes form the mononuclear phagocyte system, distributed throughout the body's connective tissues and organs.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: The gelatinous mucous connective tissue of the umbilical cord is called:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Wharton's jelly is the ground-substance-rich embryonic (mucous) connective tissue that cushions the umbilical vessels.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which adhesive glycoproteins of the ground substance anchor cells to the extracellular matrix?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Fibronectin and laminin are adhesive glycoproteins linking cells (via integrins) to the matrix and basement membrane.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: White adipose tissue is now recognised as an endocrine organ that secretes:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Adipocytes secrete adipokines such as leptin (satiety signalling) and adiponectin (insulin sensitivity), making white fat an active endocrine tissue.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Healing wounds fill with proliferating fibroblasts, new capillaries and inflammatory cells. This tissue is called:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Granulation tissue is the vascular, fibroblast-rich repair tissue of healing wounds; excess collagen later can form a keloid.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: Which collagen type is the principal fibre of hyaline cartilage?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Hyaline (and elastic) cartilage is built on type II collagen; type I predominates in bone/tendon, III in reticular tissue, IV in basement membrane.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.question: A child with recurrent long-bone fractures and blue sclerae has a defect in:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tis.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen defect (COL1A1/2) giving brittle bones and blue sclerae; fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: How is an epithelium classified/named?
options: By number of cell layers plus the shape of the surface cell
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Epithelium is named by number of layers (simple/stratified/pseudostratified) and the shape of the surface cell (squamous/cuboidal/columnar). For stratified epithelium, the surface layer determines the name.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A tissue appears layered, but every cell contacts the basement membrane and it bears cilia and goblet cells. What is it, and where is it found?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: All cells touching the basement membrane with nuclei at different heights = pseudostratified epithelium; ciliated with goblet cells, it lines the respiratory tract (nose, trachea, bronchi).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Which epithelium lines the alveoli, glomerular capsule and blood vessels, suited to diffusion and filtration?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Simple squamous epithelium — a single flat layer minimising diffusion distance — lines alveoli (gas exchange), Bowman's capsule (filtration) and vessels (endothelium).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: The epithelium of the bladder, which flattens as the organ fills, is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines the bladder and ureters; its dome-shaped umbrella cells flatten on distension, forming a stretchable, impermeable barrier.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Which epithelium provides the dry, protective surface of the skin?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium (epidermis) has a surface layer of dead, keratin-filled cells providing protection and waterproofing. Non-keratinised lines moist surfaces (mouth, oesophagus, vagina).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Which junction seals the space between epithelial cells to prevent paracellular leakage and maintain polarity?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: The tight junction (zonula occludens; claudins/occludins) seals the intercellular space, blocking paracellular movement and keeping apical and basolateral domains separate.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A patient develops flaccid intra-epidermal blisters because autoantibodies disrupt keratinocyte cell-to-cell adhesion. Which junction is targeted?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Desmosomes (cadherin–keratin spot-welds) hold keratinocytes together; anti-desmoglein autoantibodies in pemphigus vulgaris break these, causing intra-epidermal blistering.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Which structure anchors the basal epithelial cell to the basement membrane?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Hemidesmosomes use integrins to anchor the basal cell to the basement membrane. Autoimmune attack on hemidesmosome proteins (BP180/BP230) causes bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal blisters); junctional epidermolysis bullosa is an inherited hemidesmosome/BM-zone defect (EB simplex, by contrast, is a keratin 5/14 defect).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A brush border of microvilli on an absorptive cell serves to:
options: Increase apical surface area for absorption
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Microvilli (the brush/striated border, actin-cored) massively increase apical surface area for absorption — prominent in the gut and kidney proximal tubule.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A child has recurrent sinopulmonary infections, infertility and dextrocardia. Which epithelial structure is defective?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Defective ciliary dynein (primary ciliary dyskinesia) impairs mucociliary clearance and sperm motility and disturbs embryonic laterality → bronchiectasis, infertility and situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: The basement membrane stains strongly with PAS because it is rich in:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: The basal lamina is composed of type IV collagen and laminin (glycoproteins), which are PAS-positive (magenta). It attaches epithelium to connective tissue and acts as a filter.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Which gland type secretes by disintegration of the entire cell?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Holocrine secretion (sebaceous glands) involves the whole cell breaking down to release its product. Merocrine uses exocytosis; apocrine pinches off apical cytoplasm.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A goblet cell is best described as:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: A goblet cell is a single mucus-secreting cell — a unicellular exocrine gland — found in respiratory and intestinal epithelium.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: In Barrett's oesophagus, stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium. This process is called:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Metaplasia is the reversible replacement of one differentiated epithelium by another; in Barrett's, chronic acid reflux drives squamous → columnar (intestinal-type) change, a risk factor for adenocarcinoma.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A poorly differentiated tumour is cytokeratin-positive on immunohistochemistry. This indicates it is a:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Cytokeratin marks epithelial cells, so cytokeratin positivity identifies a carcinoma — the commonest group of cancers (SCC, adenocarcinoma, urothelial carcinoma).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Simple squamous epithelium lining a serous cavity (pleura, peritoneum, pericardium) is specifically called:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Mesothelium lines the serous cavities; endothelium is the equivalent simple squamous epithelium lining blood/lymphatic vessels and the heart chambers.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: The oesophagus is lined by which epithelium?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium lines the oesophagus, resisting abrasion from swallowed food while staying moist.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Tense sub-epidermal blisters in an elderly patient, with autoantibodies against hemidesmosome antigens (BP180/BP230), indicate:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosome proteins (BP180/BP230), giving tense subepidermal blisters in the elderly; pemphigus (anti-desmoglein) gives flaccid intra-epidermal blisters.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: In the apical junctional complex, the correct order from apical to basal is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: From the apex downward: tight junction (seal) → adherens junction (actin belt) → desmosome (keratin spot-welds).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A ciliated simple columnar epithelium that sweeps an ovum toward the uterus lines the:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: The uterine tube is lined by simple columnar epithelium with cilia (and secretory cells) that move the ovum toward the uterus.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Which gland type retains a duct that opens onto an epithelial surface?
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Exocrine glands keep a duct to deliver secretion onto a surface; endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: The rapid turnover/regenerative capacity of epithelium is clinically double-edged because it:
options: Enables wound healing but predisposes to carcinoma with repeated injury
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: High proliferative activity supports healing but, with chronic injury and accumulating mutations, predisposes epithelium to dysplasia and carcinoma (the commonest cancers).

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: A boy has haematuria, progressive sensorineural deafness and a family history of renal failure; renal biopsy shows basement-membrane splitting. The defective protein is:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Alport syndrome is caused by mutant type IV collagen of the basement membrane, giving GBM splitting, haematuria and sensorineural deafness.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.question: Thick viscid exocrine secretions, recurrent chest infections and pancreatic insufficiency with a raised sweat chloride are due to a defect in:
histology__BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (ty.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is a CFTR (apical chloride-channel) defect causing viscid secretions; ciliary dynein defects cause primary ciliary dyskinesia instead.

histology__BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skelet.question: A biopsy shows long, unbranched, cylindrical cells with obvious cross-striations and multiple nuclei located at the periphery just beneath the cell membrane. Which tissue is this?
